label: KVP-3600, symptom 'overtemperature_trip'
headline: Seven KVP-3600 overtemperature trips cleared by reset with zero parts and four confirmed repeats point to a fan-control firmware behaviour rather than hardware, but at 29.3 labor hours and ~3.5 MWh across two seasons this is a desk-level OEM question to fold into an existing warranty case, not a field campaign.
action: Attach the seven overtemp work orders to the already-open OEM thermal case from WO-2025-00908 and ask the vendor to confirm the current fan-control firmware baseline and whether fw 4.2.1 (seen on WO-2025-00847) is superseded, then pull firmware version during the next scheduled PM on the ~70 units in the 2024 wk18-35 band rather than dispatching for it.
reasoning: The seven members are internally coherent in a way the controls are not: every one consumed zero parts and closed as RESET / NO-FAULT-FOUND / ESCALATED (WO-2025-00449, WO-2025-00612, WO-2025-00651, WO-2025-00813, WO-2025-00847, WO-2026-00627), four explicitly record a *second* overtemp on the same asset in one season (WO-2025-00248, WO-2025-00813, WO-2025-00847, WO-2026-00627), and intakes/filters/heat sinks were recorded clear in every case where they were checked — with two independent hints at the control path (fan 'ramping late' in WO-2025-00248, 'fw 4.2.1' in WO-2025-00847). That pattern of recurring, hardware-negative resets is what a late-ramping thermal-control build looks like, and it is distinguishable from the genuine cooling-hardware failures in the control set, which did consume parts and did resolve (fan seized and replaced, WO-2025-00789; three cooling fans and an open OEM case for afternoon derate, WO-2025-00908) — so this is not simply H4 wear. H2 is weak because the events sit on seven distinct dates across four months and two calendar years and across five sites (Vireo Valley, Sandhill Bend, Tidemarsh Bay, Almond Row, Pecan Fork), not on a handful of heat days. H3 has real force — the narratives in WO-2025-00612, WO-2025-00651 and WO-2025-00449 are near-verbatim, TECH-0051 authored three members, lift is null against a 0.0 peer median, and the whole cluster is 29.3 labor hours and ~3.5 MWh across two seasons — which is exactly why this is real but not worth a campaign. All seven member serials fall in the 2024 manufacture band (weeks 18-35 if the serial encodes YYWW), while none of the older KVP-3600 controls (1813A, 1927C x2) produced an overtemp trip, which is the one thread worth pulling at desk cost.
contradicting: Three member narratives are near-verbatim duplicates and TECH-0051 authored three of seven, so part of the apparent similarity is reporting template rather than independent observation; peer median of 0.0 makes the lift uncomputable, so no true outlier status is demonstrated. Two KVP-3600 controls fall inside the same 2024 manufacture window with no overtemp trip (WO-2025-00614 on 2423B, WO-2025-00908 on 2428C), weakening a tight build-window claim. Firmware version is recorded on exactly one unit (WO-2025-00847), so the central mechanism of H1 rests on a single data point plus one tech's hunch.

population_detail.description: KVP-3600 units manufactured in 2024 weeks 18-35, the band containing all seven affected serials (2418B, 2419B, 2422B x2, 2432C x2, 2435C), out of 376 installed.
population_detail.basis: Sum of units_by_2024_manufacture_week for weeks 18 through 35 (1+6+6+7+4+3+3+4+8+2+3+4+2+8+5+1+3 = 70), assuming the serial segment encodes year-week as it does for the older controls (1813A, 1927C). Confirmed affected assets to date: 7.

hypotheses.statement: A firmware-level fan/thermal-control defect on a subset of KVP-3600 units (e.g. fw 4.2.1 ramping cooling too late) causes nuisance overtemperature trips on hot afternoons that clear on reset without any hardware fault.
predictions: Zero parts consumption across essentially all members; resolution codes dominated by RESET / NO-FAULT-FOUND / ESCALATED rather than component replacement
Repeat events on the same asset_id within a season (recurrence flag true on a majority of members) and near-zero events on units already carrying a later firmware build
Trip timestamps concentrated in the afternoon peak-load window and in the warm-season months, with no correlated fouling findings (intakes/filters recorded clear in inspection text)
Members skew toward specific serial/build prefixes (e.g. 24xxB vs 24xxC) rather than being spread uniformly across the 376-unit fleet
Lost MWh per event small (~0.5 MWh) and labor hours modest, consistent with a reset-and-go failure mode
discriminating_evidence: Firmware version recorded per asset: if affected units all sit on one build and unaffected units on another, this beats the ambient-heat and artifact explanations
Same-site, same-day work orders on non-KVP inverters: absence of thermal events on other models under identical ambient conditions rules out H2
A closed-loop test: units that receive a fan-control firmware update show no further overtemp WOs in the following warm season

hypotheses.statement: The trips are driven by a handful of discrete high-ambient-temperature days rather than by anything model-specific, and any inverter operating near its derate threshold on those days would have tripped.
predictions: Event dates cluster onto a small number of calendar days rather than spreading evenly across the warm months; multiple assets trip on or within a day of each other
Other inverter models at the same sites (Almond Row, Vireo Valley, Sandhill Bend) show thermal derate, high-cabinet-temp or overtemp work orders on those same dates
Affected sites are geographically/climatically clustered rather than randomly distributed across the portfolio
Narratives mention afternoon timing and no mechanical findings; cabinet temperature recorded as normal by the time the tech arrives
discriminating_evidence: Cross-model query on the same site-days: if peer-model overtemp WOs exist on those dates, the model attribution collapses
If the 7 events are spread across 7 distinct dates in 4 different months and 2 calendar years (as the sample suggests), a single-heat-event explanation is weakened and H1 or H3 is favoured

hypotheses.statement: This is not a real cluster: 7 events across 376 units over roughly two seasons (~1.9%, ~1%/yr) is ordinary variation, and the apparent lift is an artifact of a peer median of 0.0 produced by small peer populations plus templated narrative text that inflates apparent similarity.
predictions: Peer inverter models in the corpus have installed bases far smaller than 376, so their overtemp counts of 0-1 round to a 0.0 median and no meaningful lift can be computed (lift is already null)
Total absolute overtemp counts across all models are comparable once normalised by unit-years; KVP-3600 is simply the largest cohort and therefore the only one with enough exposure to register events

Several narratives are near-verbatim duplicates ('tripped on over temperature mid afternoon. Reset at the HMI, came back and ran the rest of the day. Nothing else in the fault log.'), indicating template or copy-paste entry rather than independent observations
A disproportionate share of members are authored by a small number of techs (TECH-0051 appears in 3 of 7), suggesting reporting behaviour rather than fleet behaviour
No parts, low total labor (29.3 h) and low lost energy (3.5 MWh) across 7 WOs — an economically negligible signal
discriminating_evidence: Unit-year-normalised overtemp rate for every inverter model with >100 units: if KVP-3600 is not an outlier once exposure is matched, the cluster is a population-size effect
Author/tech distribution: if removing the single highest-contributing tech's WOs drops the count to near peer levels, this is reporting culture, not hardware
String-similarity check on narrative text: high duplicate-fragment scores support templated entry and weaken any inference drawn from narrative content

hypotheses.statement: Cooling-path performance degrades with age on the older KVP-3600 serial blocks (fan bearing wear, heat-sink loading, thermal-paste dry-out), producing expected end-of-life-band thermal trips that superficial intake/filter checks would not detect.
predictions: Affected assets skew to the oldest serial/commissioning cohorts; newest units in the 376-unit fleet contribute no events
Recurrence interval on individual assets shortens over successive seasons (second trip closer to the first than the prior year's spacing)
Follow-up PM or escalation WOs on the same assets eventually record fan, blower or heat-sink parts consumption, even though the initial CM used no parts
Cumulative operating hours or commissioning date correlates with trip probability across the cohort
discriminating_evidence: Commissioning date / serial-age vs event incidence: a flat age profile refutes wear and points to H1 or H3
Downstream parts consumption on escalated WOs — replacement of fan or thermal hardware supports wear; a firmware push closing the escalations supports H1
Airflow or fan-speed telemetry on affected vs unaffected units of the same age: degraded measured airflow supports wear, normal airflow with late ramp timing supports the control-logic defect

exposure_note: Priced at the cost model's inverter replacement rate. This population is not inverters, so treat the count as the reliable figure and this dollar value as indicative only.
